name: Hooking
description: Adversaries may utilize hooking to hide the presence of artifacts associated with their behaviors to evade detection. Hooking can be used to modify return values or data structures of system APIs and function calls. This process typically involves using 3rd party root frameworks, such as Xposed or Magisk, with either a system exploit or pre-existing root access. By including custom modules for root frameworks, adversaries can hook system APIs and alter the return value and/or system data structures to alter functionality/visibility of various aspects of the system.

telemetry.name: Application Permission
telemetry.description: Declared or granted permissions of a mobile application.
telemetry.collection_focus: Compare manifest declarations with runtime granted state using authorized package inspection and own-app permission checks.

providers.name: Android logcat
providers.scope: Permitted logs from a consented test device/emulator; output depends on build, permissions and instrumentation.

providers.name: Android dumpsys
providers.scope: Point-in-time service/package state on an authorized development device.

providers.name: Instrumented test application
providers.scope: Own-app permission, API and state callbacks; not universal visibility into other apps.

configuration: Use a disposable emulator or owned development device with approved debugging. Record OS/API level, app version and instrumentation privileges.
Collect only relevant logcat buffers/tags and service snapshots; add explicit own-app instrumentation for events absent from OS logs.
Forward sanitized logs and compare before/after state. Remove test data and revoke debugging access after the lab session.

configuration_example.label: Inspect the owned Android lab application
configuration_example.note: Read-only snapshot on a consented debug device. Replace the example package with your owned test app. Output and access vary by Android build; this is not a permission-request event stream.

telemetry.example_note: Project-normalized synthetic JSON, not a native provider log, captured event, attack verdict or validated detection. A parser/adapter is required for a real SIEM. Example names, IPs and values are fictional.
telemetry.limitations: Android tooling does not imply iOS coverage. Standard mobile apps cannot observe all other apps or protected OS internals; MDM status is not full API, filesystem or content telemetry.
telemetry.anomaly_design: Per owned device, app version and permission state: unexpected API/permission changes, background activity and network destinations. OS privacy restrictions and emulator differences limit observability.

telemetry.name: OS API Execution
telemetry.description: Instrumented operating-system API calls and their return values.
telemetry.collection_focus: Use an approved EDR trace or instrument the owned lab process at selected APIs. Define API name, caller, sanitized arguments and return status.

providers.name: Application audit logs
providers.scope: First-party service events and request/result fields; schema is application-specific.

providers.name: OpenTelemetry-compatible log pipelines
providers.scope: Transport and normalization of emitted records; do not create missing audit instrumentation.

configuration: Enable the application audit category or instrument the owned lab application at the authorization/action boundary.
Define a schema with timestamp, service, actor, object, action, result and correlation ID. Export structured records through an authenticated collector.
Redact secrets and personal content, separate audit from debug logs, set retention and verify delivery during rotation/restart.
telemetry.example_note: Project-normalized synthetic JSON, not a native provider log, captured event, attack verdict or validated detection. A parser/adapter is required for a real SIEM. Example names, IPs and values are fictional.
telemetry.limitations: Debug output is not necessarily a durable audit trail. Application developers must emit the relevant event; installing a log pipeline does not make an absent event exist.
telemetry.anomaly_design: Per application, client and route: request rate, rare actions, failure ratios and unusual state transitions. Version changes, retries, health probes and seasonal load need separate baselines.

analytics.name: Analytic 1850
analytics.guidance: Correlates (1) device posture changes indicating root or elevated privilege state, (2) runtime framework manipulation or injection into application processes, and (3) anomalous API behavior or suppressed security signals. The defender observes a causal chain where an application gains privileged execution context, interacts with system frameworks (e.g., ART/Zygote), and modifies expected API outputs or suppresses security-relevant signals such as permission checks, sensor access reporting, or process visibility.

tuning.description: Defines correlation window between root detection, runtime manipulation, and anomalous API behavior
Baseline of known applications that legitimately use instrumentation or debugging frameworks
Determines whether suspicious API manipulation must occur in background to increase fidelity
Defines which attestation signals (Play Integrity, OEM attestation) are trusted in the environment

log_sources.name: android:MDMLog
log_sources.channel: device transitions to non-compliant state + root detected or integrity attestation failure (SafetyNet/Play Integrity)

log_sources.name: MobileEDR:telemetry
log_sources.channel: application process loads external code modules or injects into runtime (zygote/app_process) + abnormal library loading or method interception behavior

software.name: Monokle
software.description: [Monokle](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0407) can hook itself to appear invisible to the Process Manager.(Citation: Lookout-Monokle)

references.description: Bauer A., Kumar A., Hebeisen C., et al. (2019, July). Monokle: The Mobile Surveillance Tooling of the Special Technology Center. Retrieved September 4, 2019.

software.name: FjordPhantom
software.description: [FjordPhantom](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1208) has used the hooking framework in a variety of ways, including returning false information to detection mechanisms, pretending that GooglePlayServices are unavailable, and manipulating UI functionality.(Citation: Promon FjordPhantom Oct2024)

references.description: Promon Security Research Team. (2024, October 1). Retrieved February 19, 2025.

software.name: GodFather
software.description: [GodFather](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1231) has used the Xposed hooking framework to intercept HTTP requests and responses, capturing and exfiltrating sensitive information, such as credentials.(Citation: ZimperiumOrtegaPratapagiri_GodFather_Jun2025)

references.description: Ortega, F. Pratapagiri, V. (2025, June 18). Your Mobile App, Their Playground: The Dark Side of Virtualization. Retrieved July 16, 2025.
